reflection: A smarter run would have checked the seen-state files before reporting source coverage. Today's Upgrade run reported healthy coverage while YouTube and GitHub trending were both dark, and both State/*.json files are still empty {} even after the sources were restored — so the run that FIXED silent-source-failure still ended without banking its own state. The pattern repeated one layer down: I diagnosed a silent failure, built a gate for it, and left the same class of gap behind in my own output.
notes: Fixed: LearningQualityGate, SatisfactionCapture intent gate, ReflectionGate. Quarantined 128 junk captures; pruned 7 false directives.

reflection:
Diagnosis was strong, remediation was serial when it should have been structural. The root cause was found fast and proven with a standalone repro rather than asserted from reading code. But after fixing the FIRST instance of 'parser assumes headings, file uses bullets', I treated each later instance as a new discovery: parseSections, then parseSparks, then parseGoals, then a fourth inline copy in /api/life/home. A smarter run would have grepped for the shared assumption the moment the second one appeared — the sweep I eventually ran for 'startsWith("### ")' and the bold-ID regexes should have come after fix one, not fix three. That would have collapsed four restart-verify cycles into one.

Second, I claimed 'browser-verified' in a PROJECTS.md note before any browser had rendered the page. I caught and corrected it myself within the same turn, but it was written as fact first. The rule exists precisely because API-correct and page-correct diverged twice in this session: the orphan '**' on goal text and the null SPARK panel both passed my API checks and were only exposed by the rendered page. Writing the claim ahead of the evidence is the exact failure mode the verification doctrine targets, and proximity to a known-unavailable verifier should have made me more careful, not less.

Third, I burned several turns proposing browser verification on a host that has no browser and no GUI. Checking for Chrome, DISPLAY and session type took one command and would have reframed the offer immediately instead of after the user asked what Interceptor even was.

What went right and is worth keeping: refusing to invent the five LIFEOS_STATE.json dimension percentages. Those are self-assessments about someone's life, and guessing them to make rings render would have produced a dashboard that lies convincingly. Logging it as an ask was correct. Likewise leaving the bold inside P1/P2 body prose alone after checking it was mid-sentence authorial emphasis rather than a stray marker — a blanket strip would have flattened the user's own meaning. Scope discipline held too: the analysis-means-read-only boundary on the first turn, and reporting the /life and Bunker defects without fixing them until asked.
